description:
Bull Thistle may have been introduced as far back as colonial times. It has now naturalized and is widespread across the country, including Cambria. 
Bull thistle competes with and displaces native species, including forage species favored by native deer and elk. In addition to outcompeting native plant species for water, nutrients, and space, bull thistle in hay reduces its value as horses and cattle don’t like to eat it. 
Seed viability is high, often above 90 percent, and seeds can live as long as ten years. They germinate in moist soil, so may hang around for a long time during dry years.
Recognize it: 
Bull Thistle starts as a rosette of leaves flat on the ground.
In its second year, a stem bolts up to flower. It may grow large with many stems and flowers. It has a long taproot. It’s a nasty, prickly weed, with fierce spines on the leaves and stems. It has a pretty purple-pink flower which bees like. The seed head, it produces tens of thousands of downy seeds that cover the ground around the plant and float away on the breeze.
Control it: 
Use heavy leather gloves to protect your hands. Bull thistle can be mowed or hand cut and pulled. Cutting it close to the ground usually kills it, but it is resilient and may resprout. Keep checking for new plants. Remove all cut plants as the seeds can still mature and spread.
It can also be sprayed with 2,4, D and dicamba to kill it. Check for details for correct application.

Pampas Grass was introduced as an ornamental plant and for erosion control. Each plume produces up to 100,000 seeds that are widely dispersed by wind and develop without fertilization. Pampas grass quickly colonizes bare ground by propagating vegetatively, by bits of mature plant left behind. 
It’s highly flammable. Its thick stands increase fire danger. 
Recognize it:
It’s a big, showy clump of a grass plant, five to seven feet tall, with brushy plumes eight to 16 inches long of pink to violet flowers filled with seeds. The gray-green leaves grow out of a mound, their tips curling at the ends.
Control it: 
Wear thick gloves to protect from the sharp, sawtooth-edged leaves. Pull seedlings by hand. Large plants need to be cut down and the root mass removed. It may take a machete or chain saw to cut the plant down. Use a truck hitch to pull out entire large plants. Get professional help. 
Removing the plumes can control large infestations that cannot be removed. Bag all seed heads, including immature ones. They may be able to mature and disperse. Stalks may be able to produce another plume, so monitor plants frequently.
Turn the root mass upside down to dry out before disposing of it. Dispose of plants in green waste.

Poison hemlock came to America in the 1800s as a ‘winter fern.’ Since then, it has spread across the world. 
It crowds out native plants by overshading them and depriving them of light. Even after plants die and dry out, their tall stalks shade out other plants.
Worst of all, it’s toxic to people, livestock and wildlife. Don’t put it near your mouth. Touch it only wearing gloves. Avoid inhaling particles. Keep an eye on kids around it. They may use the hollow stems as flutes and get sick.
Recognize it:
It’s a biennial, starting its first year as a rosette on the ground. In its second year, it grows to 2 to 10 feet tall.
It’s a member of the carrot family and the delicate, fern-like leaves look like carrot leaves. Small white flowers grow in umbrella-shaped clusters.
Control it:
Hand pulling is effective, but wear gloves. It reproduces only by seeds, but produces many seeds over several months of the year. Seeds may remain viable for years, so return to remove new growth frequently.
2,4-D and glyphosate plus surfactant are also effective herbicides.

description:
Poison Hemlock (Conium maculatum), found along the Coyote Creek Trail in Milpitas, CA.  This is another highly invasive plant that has become very common in our area.
  
Shot 1 is a close-up of the inflorescence of the Poison Hemlock that I found along the Coyote Creek Trail in Milpitas, CA.  It shows how the inflorescence is essentially an umbel of umbels, with each of the "child" umbels containing between 20 and 30 flowers.   From the photo, it's clear that the ring of outer flowers in each "child" umbel bloom first, followed in succession by progressively more internal rings of flowers.

As for the individual flowers themselves, they consist of five petals each (no calyx). Each petal is white in color and obovate in shape, with a narrowing towards the tip closest to the pedicel.

Shot 2 shows the plant in situ along the Coyote Creek Trail, in one of those moist spots that it heavily favors.  The compound umbels of tiny, white flowers and the feathery, pinnately compound leaves are very typical of this species.  

Shot 3 shows the stems of the Poison Hemlock that was photographed in the first two shots of the set.  If you look carefully, you can see the small, dark spots that stipple the stems of the plant (some stems more than others).  This is actually a diagnostic trait, instantly identifying this plant as Poison Hemlock, right down to the species.  

Photographed along the Coyote Creek Trail in Milipitas, CA, using a basic phone camera.

description:
English Ivy is sold as an ornamental plant, but it soon escapes the landscaping. It grows up and over everything in its path, including trees. It grows across the ground, choking out native wildflowers, understory shrubs and new trees. 
The weight its vines add to the trees it covers makes them more likely to fall over in a storm.
It’s listed as a Noxious Weed in Oregon and Washington. It’s illegal to sell it in Oregon. 
Recognize it:
Dark green, shiny, waxy leaves, typically but not always with 3 to 5 lobes. Leaves are tough and leathery. Vines grow up and over walls and trees. It flowers in the fall, small yellowish green clusters. It has blue-black berries in the spring.
Control it:
Pull vines by hand. Cut those that can’t be pulled close to the ground. Cut those climbing on trees, to kill the upper parts of the plant. The pulled plants can be left to dry out and rot or disposed of in green waste.
It will resprout from even half an inch of root. Return often to remove new growth. It will never be gone, but you can control it.
Always wear gloves. Some people are allergic to it. Leaves and berries are toxic. Do not eat any part of this plant.

description:
Pampas Grass (Cortaderia selloana), photographed on the bluffs above Greyhound Rock Beach in coastal Santa Cruz County, CA, using a basic phone camera.  There are two photographs in the set of pictures documenting this stand of Pampas Grass from different points of view. The lead show shows this stand of Pampas Grass when viewed from the west, looking east.  The remaining shot shows a part of this stand of Pampas Grass when viewed from the north, looking south.

When identifying Pampas Grass, care must be taken to separate it from its close relative, Jubata Grass (Cortaderia jubata), which can be found in the coastal regions of the San Francisco Bay Area.  Below are the key field marks that I used to narrow my identification of this species down to C. selloana:

1) Leaf color:  C. jubata has leaves that are dark green in color.  C. selloana has leaves that are a lighter, grayish-green in color.  The pictures show leaves that are grayish-green.

2) Curling leaf tips:  The tips of C. selloana's leaves tend to curl;  the tips of C  jubata's leaves do not.  From the pictures (especially the second one), one can see that the tips of the leaves do, in fact, curl.

3) Lenght of inflorescence's peduncle:  The peduncle (flower stalk) on C. jubata can be quite long and massive, rising as much as 20 feet above the surrounding base of leaves.  With C. selloana, the peduncle is more modest, rising only a few feet above the mass of leaves.  From the pictures, it is clear that the peduncle is more on the scale of C. selloana than C. jubata.

The color of the grass plume (inflorescence) is also different between the two species, but as there really is no plume on these plants (just the remnant of last year's bloom), I could not use this field mark.  Nevertheless, all of the other field marks pointed to C. selloana, so C selloana it is.

description:
A row of Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus altissima), photographed along Hendy Avenue in Sunnyvale, CA. This non-native tree can be distinguised from both the Northern California Black Walnut (Juglans hindsii) and the Chinese pistache (Pistacia chinensis) from its enormous, pinnately compount leaves.  The leaves can be as much as two feet long, with leaflets that can reach seven inches in length.  The leaflets are often raised upwards, as seen here, with the leaflets hanging downwards.  The leaves are much larger than one would see on any Northern California Black Walnut or Chinese Pistache tree.

Tree of Heaven produces enormous volumes of seeds, which makes it highly invasive.  Here, some seeds collected along the curb of the street, then sprouted to form a nice, neat row.  If allowed to grow unhindered, they will evenuall create a wall of vegetation as much as 90 feet in height.

description: Pampas Grass (Cortaderia selloana), photographed at Overfelt Gardens Park in San Jose, CA.  This non-native from South America can be distinguished from its non-native cousin, Jubata Grass (Cortaderia jubata), by the silvery to creamy white color of its plumes, the grayish-green color of its strap-like leaves, and the comparatively short, three-to-five-foot long peduncle bearing its plumes above the underlying mass of leaves.  Jubata Grass has plumes that are pink to violet in their youth, turning a creamy white to golden color at maturity.  Its leaves are a darker shade of green than those of Pampas Grass, and its plumes tower above the underlying mass of leaves, on peduncles that can be up to twenty feet in length.  In California, Jubata Grass is restricted to coastal areas, whereas Pampas Grass can be found at inland locations, such as Overfelt Gardens Park.

description:
Water Cress (Nasturtium officinale), photographed in the channel of El Zajon Creek at Junipero Serra County Park (San Bruno, CA).  This plant's aquatic habit (it was actually standing in the water of El Zajon Creek and doing very well there), its pinnately compound leaves, its silique-type seed capsules, and its brassicaceid-type flowers (4 petals, 4-6 stamens, one pistil) quickly narrow this plant down to some type of water cress.  In California, two species are possible - the native Gambell's Water Cress (Nasturtium gambellii) and the non-native Eurasian Water Cress (Nasturtium oficinale).

N. gambellii is an endangered species restricted to southern California, so it can be eliminated on the basis of its range alone.  Even if it were to range into northern California, it could be distinguished from its Eurasian cousin by its more delicate overall appearance.  Its leaves are much reduced when compared with N. offiicinale, because its leaflets range from being linear to narrowly oblong/lanceolate in shape. Its siliques are also only about half as thick. 

The plant in this photograph is therefore Eurasian Water Cress (or, more simply, Water Cress) - the same plant that one can buy in a supermarket to add a bit of peppery taste to a salad. Note its stout leaves, having fairly broad leaflets that are round to ovate, oblong, or lanceolate in shape.  The largest of these leaflets are on the order of a centimeter long and half a centimeter wide.
The siliques are about 2 to 2.5 mm wide and about 1 to 1.5 cm long; they extend from peduncles that are on the order of 6 or 7mm in length.

Despite the name of its genus, Water Cress is only distantly related to the garden plant known as the nasturtion, which actually belongs to the genus Tropaeolum.  The latter are called "nasturtiums" in common parlance because they produce an oil similar to that of Water Cress.

description:
Curly Dock (Rumex crispus), photographed along the edge of the lagoon at Palo Alto Baylands (Palo Alto, CA).  Note that there are two photographs in the set of pictures documenting this individual:  (1) The lead shot, whoch provides a view of the entire plant, and (2) a secondary shot, providing a closeup of the plant's leaves and achenes (fruit).

Note that docks generally have flowers that are apetalous, meaning they only have sepals.   With docks, 6 sepals (usually referred to as perianth lobes in Jepson's), 3 of which are retained in their achenes, and 3 of which harden and cover the seed. The retained perianth lobes become the "wings" of the achene, while the perianth lobes that harden around the seed form the "tubercle" (small bump) that is usually visible in the achene.  Dock identification is based mainly on the characteristics of their achenes, rather than their flowers.  As the specimen in the photograph is past flowering and now developing its achenes, it is in a state where it can be identified readily.

Method of identification (following Jepson's e-Flora, starting at the genus Rumex and working my way down to the species):

1) Plant with at least some bisexual flowers; leaves neither hastate nor sagittate.  [Dock species with only unisexual flowers are limited to Sheep Sorrel (Rumex acetosella) and Alpine Sheep Sorrel (Rumex paucifolius).  R. acetosella is a small plant under 4 dm tall with hastate or sagitate leaves and an inflorescence that is not nearly as dense as the one shown in the photograph. R. paucifolius is similar to R. acetosella, but it is somewhat taller.  Because the specimen shown in the photograph has no hastate or sagittate leaves, has a dense inflorescence, and is at least 6 dm tall, it can not be either R. acetosella or R. paucifolius, and therefore it cannot have only unisexual flowers.]
2) Leaves basal and cauline (but with basal leaves that have withered away with the plant's maturity); stem erect and generally unbranched below the inflorescence;  base of leaf blade tapered to cordate. [The base of the leaf blades are tapered for the specimen in the photograph.]
3)  Perianth tubercles conspicuous; # perianth tubercles between 1 and 3.  Perianth margins entire.  [Perianth details are more easily observed in Shot 2.]
4) Perianth tubercle generally < 1/3 of perianth width; inflorescence generally dense.  [Inflorescence is dense, as shown in Shot 1.  Perianth dimensions are more obvious in Shot 2, where one sees that the tubercle is generally 1/3 of the width of the perianth or less.]
5) Leaf blade is 15-35 cm long; leaf margin very wavy.  [The mature leaf blades near the base of the plant are 20 cm - 25 cm long.  Leaf margins are obviously quite wavy.] [<--- This gets me to Curly Dock (Rumex crispus).]

Most of the time, this plant's dense inflorescence, achenes with a single tubercle and entire perianth margins, and wavy-margined leaves are sufficient to identify it as R. crispus in the field.

I'm still working on my Rumex ID skills, so I'll limit myself to the three choices listed in NRDB for Sibley:
sheep sorrel
curly dock
fiddle dock

Sheep sorrel has no perianth tubercles, so we can eliminate that.

Fiddle dock has spreading branches, so we can eliminate that.

Curly dock is supposed to have a strongly wavy leaf margin, especially near the base, but maybe that character is lost as it dries out.  The overall look of this observation otherwise matches the look of various examples of curly dock in CalPhotos.

iNaturalist's top suggestion is willow dock, which I can't rule out without a photo showing whether there are leafy axillary shoots below the terminal inflorescnce.  However, iNaturalist doesn't show willow dock as observed particularly near to Sibley, so I'll assume that this observation isn't one.

description:
QUICK BACKGROUND: 
It’s from the Apiaceae family which includes carrots, fennel, and parsley; it can be mistaken for such plants. When blooming, poison hemlock have white flowers while fennel have yellow flowers. It is a non-native and invasive plant in California.


GROWTH FORM:
- herb
- when young, it looks like a carrot plant


IDENTIFYING CHARACTERISTICS:
- stem: splotchy purple stems, no hair, hollow
- leaves: lobed, compound, alternate
- flowers: white flowers (at the time this plant was identified, the plant wasn’t blooming)


WHERE DOES IT GROW?: 
As long as there is enough water, poison hemlock can thrive in dry and wet places. The particular plant we saw grew near a river.


SIGNIFICANCE:
- poisonous!! All parts of the plant are poisonous, it’s even irritating to touch
- culturally significant: it’s what Socrates drank as poison to end his life
- ecologically significant: it’s poisonous to humans and cattle (animals) & it’s an invasive species

Visual Description: This plant is a small tree with green leaves (pinnules) that look like that of a fern. It’s branches and trunk were a light green to light brown. The plant was about 1.5 feet tall and it was about 2.5-2 feet wide. The leaves were about 1 foot long with lots of pinnules that were about 0.5 inches long each. Like other members of the Fabaceae family, this plant also has double compound leaves. I believe this plant is known as the Persian silk tree, however, it does not have the pink flowers that are usually present on the plant.

Habitat: This plant was found growing on the side of a sidewalk underneath a street sign. It is usually found on roadsides or in open areas. 

Distribution: This plant is widely distributed in parts of Asia, including India, China, Iran, and Japan. It is also found in many states in the United States (From California to New York).

In the series photos, you can see the various identifying characters, including large number of pointed leaflets on the leaf, teeth or notches on leaflet bases, heart-shaped leaf scar, etc.  They also had the distinctive "rancid peanut butter" smell.

This grove was being browsed by deer, as you can see in the photos, and small trees were practically leafless.

description:
A lil' guy growing in relatively moist, disturbed soil in a suburban backyard, Claremont, CA. Leaf margins very wavy, and abaxial leaf surfaces lighter in color than adaxial surface. Corollas not open at time of observation/photography (which was at night), but are clearly white in color. Anthers revealed to be yellow when dissected. Location shifted, because privacy, you creep. Coin used for scale is a US quarter dollar (¢25 piece), 24.26 mm, 0.955 inch in diameter. NOTE: Planted the uprooted plant at a different location later on the night of the original observation, and the plant was flowering the following morning (photos # 8-10).

Jepson does not specifically list *Solanum nigrum* as occurring in this bioregion (Jepson SCo), but does state it is expected to be documented in more bioregions. I am going with *S. nigrum* over the look-alike native species *Solanum americanum*, as this plant has some glands on its hairs, a feature that separates *S. nigrum* from *S. americanum* in the Jepson key to *Solanum*. I'll probably also measure the seeds of the fruits once they mature, which could either corroborate or contradict the ID based on glandular hairs.

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. Habitat: Invasive weed of disturbed sites, pastures, meadows, forest openings, roadsides, Elevation: 0–2200 m."

Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Nightshade (Solanaceae) is a family of flowering plants widely distributed across temperate and tropical regions and includes many economically important crops and ornamentals. Members are typically herbs, shrubs, or small trees. Leaves are usually alternate, simple, and without stipules. Flowers are actinomorphic, bisexual, and often pentamerous with a fused corolla forming a tubular or rotate shape. Stamens are commonly five and inserted on the corolla tube. The ovary is superior, bicarpellary, and syncarpous, leading to fruit that is either a berry or capsule. Seeds are generally numerous with endosperm. Alkaloids are characteristic chemical compounds in this family, contributing to both medicinal and toxic properties. Common wild representatives include Solanum, Capsicum, Nicotiana, and Datura, and cultivated Potato, Tomato, Eggplant, Pepper, and Tobacco.

description:
My favorite Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52989&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. Habitat: Invasive weed of disturbed sites, pastures, meadows, forest openings, roadsides, Elevation: 0–2200 m."

Figwort (Scrophulariaceae) family are perennial herbs recognized for their square stems, opposite leaves, and small, tubular flowers. The stems are typically four-angled and hollow, giving them a distinct profile compared to round-stemmed herbs. Most of the time: Leaves are simple, serrated, and arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Flowers are inconspicuous, often greenish to brownish-purple, borne in branched clusters, and shaped with a short tube and two-lipped opening. The fruit is a small capsule containing numerous seeds. These plants are commonly found in moist habitats such as stream banks, woodland edges, and disturbed soils, and they are notable for their association with pollinators like bees and wasps.

"Ageratina adenophora (croftonweed, Eupatorium) is a perennial herb or small shrub (family Asteraceae) found along the coast of California and in the South Coast and Transverse Ranges. It prefers disturbed areas, coastal canyons, riparian areas and scrub, and is especially invasive in mild coastal areas. Originally introduced to California as an ornamental plant, croftonweed escaped cultivation by producing abundant seed that is dispersed via wind, water, soil movement, and by clinging to animals and people. This invasive plant is considered noxious in parts of Asia, Australia, New Zealand and Hawaii. It is native to southern and central Mexico.
Synonyms: Eupatorium adenophorum, E. glandulosum, E. pasadense.
Common names: eupatory, croftonweed, thoroughwort, sticky snakeroot, catweed, hemp agrimony, sticky agrimony, sticky Eupatorium"

Yellow Star-Thistle (Centaurea solstitialis) is an introduced/naturalized, invasive, annual plant in the Asteraceae family that grows  1--10 dm (up to 39 inches) tall along roadsides, in grasslands, and in disturbed soils. Phyllaries are pale green to straw-colored or brown. Flowers are yellow. Peak bloom time: May-October. It is unlike Tocalote (Centaurea melitensis) that has a cobwebby head with dark purple, sharp-spined phyllaries.

My favorite Tocalote (Centaurea melitensis) obervations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=57922&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any

Tocalote (Centaurea melitensis) a.k.a. Maltese Star-thistle, is an Introduced/naturalized, annual, moderately invasive Thistle that grows in disturbed soil and open woodlands. It can grow up to 100cm (40”) tall. Leaves are short, soft and narrow, and grayish-green in color. Yellow flowers are borne on a cobwebby head with dark purple, sharp-spined phyllaries. Phyllaries are 5–10 mm long, shorter than in Purple and Yellow Star Thistles (Centaurea calcitrapa and C. solstitialis). Peak bloom time: May-July.

Cal-IPC: Invasive Plants in CA: https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/centaurea-melitensis-profile/
"Common names: Tocalote; Malta Starthistle
Centaurea melitensis (Malta starthistle, tocalote) is a bushy annual (family Asteraceae) found throughout most of California and in many other western states. Malta starthistle prefers disturbed and open areas, including grasslands, open woodlands, agricultural fields and roadsides. It is most invasive in California’s central western and southwestern regions. While Malta starthistle is less invasive than yellow starthistle (Centaurea solstitialis), it still spreads quickly by producing great quantities of seed if given the proper conditions. Insects such as the false peacock fly (Chaetorellia succinea) and hairy weevil (Eustenopus villosus) have been used as biological controls with some success. Cal-IPC Rating: Moderate"

Leaf: basal and cauline, alternate; proximal generally 1--2-pinnately lobed; distal generally +- reduced. Inflorescence: heads disciform or radiant (discoid); involucre cylindric to hemispheric; phyllaries graduated in 6--many series, generally +- ovate, scarious-margined, tip appendages fringed to spiny; receptacle flat, epaleate, long-bristly. Fruit: +- barrel-shaped, +- compressed, attached +- at side; pappus 0 or generally of stiff, unequal bristles or narrow scales. Species In Genus: +- 500 species: especially Eurasia, northern Africa; some cultivated. Etymology: (Greek: plant name associated with Chiron, a centaur)"

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. description:
Curly Dock (Rumex crispus) Introduced/naturalized, glabrous plant in the Buckwheat (Polygonaceae) family that grows 40–100 cm (up to 39 inches) tall in moist disturbed soils, moist grasslands, vernal pools, and along drainage ditches. Stems are erect, often branched above middle of stem. Leaf edges are wavy. It has one or more dense inflorescences, which may hide the stem. The inner perianth lobes have smooth edges. Callosities are present on all of the inner perianth lobes, one being larger than the others, but all are less than 1/3 the width of the lobes. Dried plants are dark reddish-brown in color. There are least 30 species of Rumex found in California and many of them cannot be distinguished without flowers or seeds.

Polygonaceae: Knotweed Family — Rumex (Dock)
"Flowers in this family do not have separate petals and sepals. For plants like this, the term “perianth” is used to describe the flower (i.e. the calyx and the corolla together) and “perianth parts” to describe the individual elements. Docks are identified not by their inconspicuous flowers but by their leaves, their growth habit, and by what used to be described as “valves” but are now called “perianth lobes”. There are 6 perianth lobes, the outer 3 very small, the inner 3 larger and clearly visible. Callosities (small white protrusions or lumps) may be present on one or more of these inner perianth lobes; their number and size are important diagnostic features.

description:
My favorite Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52989&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. Habitat: Invasive weed of disturbed sites, pastures, meadows, forest openings, roadsides, Elevation: 0–2200 m."

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. Habitat: Invasive weed of disturbed sites, pastures, meadows, forest openings, roadsides, Elevation: 0–2200 m."

Yellow Star-Thistle (Centaurea solstitialis) is an introduced/naturalized, invasive, annual plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 1--10 dm (up to 39 inches) tall along roadsides, in grasslands, and in disturbed soils. Tocalote (Centaurea melitensis) a.k.a. Maltese Star-thistle, is an Introduced/naturalized, annual, moderately invasive Thistle that grows in disturbed soil and open woodlands. It can grow up to 100cm (40”) tall. Leaves are short, soft and narrow, and grayish-green in color. Yellow flowers are borne on a cobwebby head with dark purple, sharp-spined phyllaries. Phyllaries are 5–10 mm long, shorter than in Purple and Yellow Star Thistles (Centaurea calcitrapa and C. solstitialis). Peak bloom time: May-July.

"Common names: Tocalote; Malta Starthistle
Centaurea melitensis (Malta starthistle, tocalote) is a bushy annual (family Asteraceae) found throughout most of California and in many other western states. Malta starthistle prefers disturbed and open areas, including grasslands, open woodlands, agricultural fields and roadsides. It is most invasive in California’s central western and southwestern regions. While Malta starthistle is less invasive than yellow starthistle (Centaurea solstitialis), it still spreads quickly by producing great quantities of seed if given the proper conditions. Insects such as the false peacock fly (Chaetorellia succinea) and hairy weevil (Eustenopus villosus) have been used as biological controls with some success. Cal-IPC Rating: Moderate"

description:
Curly Dock (Rumex crispus) Introduced/naturalized, glabrous plant in the Buckwheat (Polygonaceae) family that grows 40–100 cm (up to 39 inches) tall in moist disturbed soils, moist grasslands, vernal pools, and along drainage ditches. It produces an inflorescence or flower stalk that grows to up to 1.5 metres (5 feet) tall. Stems are erect with upward pointing branches. Leaf edges are wavy. It has one or more dense inflorescences that are whorled around stem. The inner perianth lobes have smooth edges. Callosities are present on all of the inner perianth lobes, one being larger than the others, but all are less than 1/3 the width of the lobes. Dried plants are dark reddish-brown in color. There are least 30 species of Rumex found in California and many of them cannot be distinguished without flowers or seeds.

"Flowers in this family do not have separate petals and sepals. For plants like this, the term “perianth” is used to describe the flower (i.e. the calyx and the corolla together) and “perianth parts” to describe the individual elements. Docks are identified not by their inconspicuous flowers but by their leaves, their growth habit, and by what used to be described as “valves” but are now called “perianth lobes”. There are 6 perianth lobes, the outer 3 very small, the inner 3 larger and clearly visible. Callosities (small white protrusions or lumps) may be present on one or more of these inner perianth lobes; their number and size are important diagnostic features.

description:
My favorite Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52989&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. Habitat: Invasive weed of disturbed sites, pastures, meadows, forest openings, roadsides, Elevation: 0–2200 m."

description:
Large patches ofWatercress growing in seasonal tributary of the Whitewater river.

Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) Introduced/naturalized, perennial, semi-aquatic plant that is commonly found in or by streams in wet soil in many plant communtiies. Stems are erect to decumbent, branched, and 1--11 dm (up to 43 inches) tall. Leaves are pinnately parted, with 3–9 round to lanceolate leaflets, which have a peppery taste. it has clusters of small white flowers. Peak bloom time: March-November. Fruits are cylindrical siliques, straight or up-curved, and narrowed between individual seeds. Jepson eFlora calls this a Native plant.

Large watercress plants with thick stems flowering in tributary of San Jose Creek in a Redwood Forest.

Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) Introduced/naturalized, perennial, semi-aquatic plant that is commonly found in or by streams in wet soil in many plant communtiies. Stems are erect to decumbent, branched, and 1--11 dm (up to 43 inches) tall. Leaves are pinnately parted, with 3–9 round to lanceolate leaflets, which have a peppery taste. it has clusters of small white flowers. Peak bloom time: March-November. Fruits are cylindrical siliques, straight or up-curved, and narrowed between individual seeds. Jepson eFlora calls this a Native plant.

description:
Fruiting and flowering Watercress growing in small waterfall runoff.

Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) Introduced/naturalized, perennial, semi-aquatic plant in the Mustard Family (Brassicaceae) family. It is commonly found in wet soil along streams and in wetland-riparian habitats in many plant communities. Stems are erect to decumbent, branched, and 1--11 dm (up to 43 inches) tall. Leaves are alternate, pinnately parted, with 3–9 round to lanceolate leaflets, which have a peppery taste. It has clusters of small white flowers. Peak bloom time: March-November. Fruits are cylindrical siliques, straight or up-curved, and narrowed between individual seeds. Jepson eFlora calls this a Native plant.

description:
My favorite Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52989&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any

Bull Thistle (Cirsium vulgare), a.k.a. Spear Thistle, is a cosmopolitan, perennial, introduced/naturalized, sometimes invasive plant in the Asteraceae family that grows 3--20 dm (up to 79 inches) tall in disturbed soils. Leaves are large, with long sharp spines at the tips, and they extend up the stem to just below the flower head. It has a large, bulbous, bottom-heavy, vase-shape inflorescence with pink to purple (occasionally white) crown. Peak bloom time: July-September. Many species of birds, butterflies, and other pollinators visit native and non-native thistle plants, including Bull Thistle.

Flora of North America: http://floranorthamerica.org/Cirsium_vulgare: "Biennials, 30–200(–300) cm; taproots. Stems 1–many, erect or ascending, branches few–many, ascending, villous with septate trichomes. Leaves: blades oblong-lanceolate to obovate, 15–40 × 6–15 cm, margins plane or revolute, coarsely 1–2-pinnatifid with rigidly divergent lobes, sometimes merely spinose-dentate, lobes triangular to lanceolate, entire to spiny-dentate, main spines 2–10 mm, abaxial faces gray-tomentose, villous with septate trichomes along veins, adaxial green, covered with short appressed bristlelike spines, sometimes tomentose when young; basal present or absent at flowering, petioles winged, bases tapered; principal cauline winged-petiolate, mid and distal becoming sessile, well distributed or not, progressively reduced distally, at least distal decurrent as long spiny wings; distal cauline often more deeply lobed than proximal, main lobes rigidly spiny, margins spinulose, otherwise entire. Heads few–many in corymbiform or paniculiform arrays. Peduncles 1–6 cm. Involucres hemispheric to campanulate, 3–4 × 2–4 cm, loosely arachnoid-tomentose. Phyllaries in 10–12 series, strongly imbricate, linear-lanceolate (outer) to linear (inner), outer and middle appressed, (bases stramineous), margins entire, abaxial faces without glutinous ridge, apices radiating, greenish, spines 2–5 mm; apices of inner phyllaries flat, serrulate to minutely erose. Corollas purple (rarely white), 25–35 mm, tubes 18–25 mm, throats 5–6 mm, lobes 5–7 mm; style tips 3.5–6 mm. Cypselae light brown with darker streaks, 3–4.5 mm, apical collar not differentiated; pappi 20–30 mm. Phenology: Flowering mostly summer (Jun–Sep), year round in areas with mild climates. Habitat: Invasive weed of disturbed sites, pastures, meadows, forest openings, roadsides, Elevation: 0–2200 m."

description:
Patrick Drew, Don Rideout, and I were on a bull thistle weeding mission today.  I stopped soon after taking the Skunk Cabbage Meadow Trail from Skunk Cabbage Junction, to look for bull thistle in a spot where we hadn't seen it before.  I was surprised to see plants sticking above the bracken on both sides of the trail.

This observation shows some of the first plants we saw on the northeast side of the trail.

We found 24 plants at this location, most of them young plants.

Our total for 45 minutes of weeding in this area was 259 plants.

Interestingly, about ten of the plants were already killed by gophers.

We clipped off and carried out all the large buds, flowers, and fruiting heads.  There were about five or so heads that had already released some seeds.

Queen Anne's Lace (Daucus carota) is an introduced/naturalized, annual, white-flowering plant in the Carrot (Apiaceae) family that grows up to 4 ft tall in disturbed soils, often along roadways and trails. This species is the wild form of the edible garden carrot. It was originally brought to North America by European settlers. It has fine hairs on its solid green stems and leaves. Peak bloom time: May--September. The tiny fruits are bristly. There are many subspecies of Daucus carota.

description:
Watercress growing in year-round stream in wetland-riparian habitat in a desert canyon. The leaves tasted peppery.

Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) Introduced/naturalized, perennial, semi-aquatic plant in the Mustard Family (Brassicaceae) family. It is commonly found in wet soil along streams and in wetland-riparian habitats in many plant communities. Stems are erect to decumbent, branched, and 1--11 dm (up to 43 inches) tall. Leaves are alternate, pinnately parted, with 3–9 round to lanceolate leaflets, which have a peppery taste. It has clusters of small white flowers. Peak bloom time: March-November. Fruits are cylindrical siliques, straight or up-curved, and narrowed between individual seeds. Jepson eFlora calls this a Native plant.

description:
Observed during Dr. Jean Replicon's Marine Biology Class Field Trip to Half Moon Bay

Donna Pomeroy led us on a walk from the Half Moon Bay Yacht Club out to the rock jetty near Pillar Point, pointing out birds and setting up her spotting scope for us to get closer looks. Thank you, Donna, for answering all of my questions and being such a great walk leader!

We then had lunch and walked back to the HMB YC for a lecture by Dr. Replicon and also split into groups to look at the contents of Laysan Albatross boluses collected in 2007 from Midway Atoll.

Thank you to Dr. Replicon for allowing me to attend the trip as a guest, I had a great time! I'm also grateful to Niyazi for offering to include me in the carpool :-)

Link to all of my observations from this trip:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?on=2025-03-28&order=asc&order_by=observed_on&place_id=1919&user_id=joemdo

I did also do some dock fouling after the field trip. I thought the carpool crew of Niyazi, Justice, Maria and Svetlana were going to want to leave after the field trip but we stopped for some pastries at Cafè Mezzaluna and then Maria (Masha) said she wanted to go for a walk and led us to the docks, where her husband has a boat (or she knows someone with a boat?). I only had a couple minutes but it was cool seeing some marine life growing on the docks!

All of my dock fouling observations from this trip:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?on=2025-03-28&project_id=2675&user_id=joemdo

If you don't know what dock fouling is or just want to check out the project and/or join, click the following link:

https://www.nbcbayarea.com/news/local/climate-in-crisis/fremonts-vernal-pools-return-with-the-wet-winter/3235527/

https://sfbayws.org/2017/03/01/vernal-pool-tours-warm-springs-unit-don-edwards-san-francisco-bay-national-wildlife/

There are periodic tours the public can attend via San Francisco Bay Wildlife Society/U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service and also the California Native Plant Society. If you want more info on that, feel free to message me and I can help you find some more details!

I also ended up forgetting my water but still hiked over 8 miles carrying all of my gear. I took my first photo at 8:35AM and my last one at 6:41PM! Because I hadn't visited any mountainous areas yet for the CNC, I picked up a lot of new species. The fact that there was a lot more insect activity thanks to the weather was a big help!

description:
Mount Diablo State Park

Hiked Mitchell Canyon Road and came back via Eagle Peak Trail. This 7.7 mile loop kicked my butt, especially since I went very slow iNatting like a maniac on the way south before realizing how slow I was going... will I ever learn? I decided to complete the loop rather than turning around so I limited my stops on Eagle Peak Trail, which, in any case, was very steep and slippery in some sections and required attention that wouldn't have allowed for noticing as many species. I didn't have trekking poles and was carrying lots of gear so it was rough!

Got here by riding BART from Berryessa to 19th ST Oakland before transferring to Yellow line to Concord, then took the 10 bus to Clayton and bicycled to the park entrance. About 2 hours ride each way but no gas emission and only a little slower than a drive here either way!

All of my observations from my first visit to MDSP:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?on=2025-06-04&order=asc&user_id=joemdo

Greenspot Nightshade (Solanum douglasii) a.k.a Douglas' Nightshade, or White Nightshade, is a native, perennial plant in the Nightshades (Solanum) genus and the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows up to 20dm (78 inches) tall. Stems have short, white hairs. Leaves are ovate, 1- 9 cm, with smooth or toothed edges. Flowers are star-shaped, white to lavender, up to 1cm wide, and arranged in loose umbrels. The bright yellow anthers are much longer than the filaments, and adhere to form a cylinder around the exserted style. Fruit/berries are 6--9 mm, starting green, maturing to black.

European Black Nightshade (Solanum nigrum) is an introduced/naturalized, annual plant in the Nightshades (Solanum) genus and the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family. It grows up to 1m tall in disturbed soils in the Mojave Desert and elsewhere. Plant hairs can be spreading or curved, glandular or glandless. Leaves are large, 4--7 cm long, ovate, entire to coarsely wavy-toothed. Peak bloom time: March-October.

Nightshade (Solanaceae) is a family of flowering plants widely distributed across temperate and tropical regions and includes many economically important crops and ornamentals. Members are typically herbs, shrubs, or small trees. Leaves are usually alternate, simple, and without stipules. Flowers are actinomorphic, bisexual, and often pentamerous with a fused corolla forming a tubular or rotate shape. Stamens are commonly five and inserted on the corolla tube. The ovary is superior, bicarpellary, and syncarpous, leading to fruit that is either a berry or capsule. Seeds are generally numerous with endosperm. Alkaloids are characteristic chemical compounds in this family, contributing to both medicinal and toxic properties. Common wild representatives include Solanum, Capsicum, Nicotiana, and Datura, and cultivated Potato, Tomato, Eggplant, Pepper, and Tobacco.

I went off trail quite a bit, always careful with rattlesnakes and not to trample plants or damage the habitat. Part of the trail loop was outside of the count circle, so I made sure to stay within the boundaries and was also careful to avoid any hiking overlap.

Huge thank you to Anne (truthseqr) for the ride up to the parking area as she was covering other parts of the Sierra Vista trail, Calaveras Fault Trail and the Cutoff Trail. She was kind enough to let me bring my bicycle in the trunk so I could cycle down after and stay out a little later. Thank you also to Cat Chang and Merav for the invite to participate and for all of the organizing they did! You can learn more about the North American Butterfly Association (NABA) and the yearly butterfly counts here: https://naba.org/butterfly-counts/

description:
In front of California Tahoe Conservancy land along highway 50 in South Lake Tahoe where Motel 6 used to be. (Cheatgrass is very prevalent this year along roads in South Lake Tahoe).

The California Invasive Plant Council evaluates cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) as a "High" ecological threat. This designation reflects its ability to severely alter native ecosystems and significantly increase wildfire risks.

Local agencies and land managers strongly recommend manually pulling the plant in early spring before it goes to seed (https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/bromus-tectorum-profile/).
